walkthroughs.title: Four things to read in any fall
steps: Every big fall has a depth, a length, a cause and an aftermath. Read all four before you call it.
Depth first. The S&P 500 fell 57% from its 2007 peak to its 2009 trough. From 2000 to 2002, 49.1%.
Then length. In 2020 the fall took 33 days. The 2000 to 2002 slide ground on for 30.5 months.
Cause tells you what broke. Aftermath tells you how long the repair took.

walkthroughs.title: Stocks and the economy keep different clocks
steps: March 2009, the S&P 500 hits its trough. The recession doesn't end until June.
2002 ran the other way. The recession ended in November 2001, and stocks still slid to new lows by October 2002.
Both times the official end date came out over a year later. By then, price had long since moved.

walkthroughs.title: A bounce is not a bottom
steps: January 2022, the S&P 500 closes at a record, 4,796.56. By mid-June it's down to 3,666.77.
Then it bounces for two months, all the way up to 4,305.20 in mid-August. Feels like the bottom's in.
October 12 it closes at 3,577.03, a new low. That was the real bottom, and you only knew it in hindsight.

questions.q: Four big S&P 500 falls since 2000. Which one took the most off the index, from peak to low?
questions.why: The 2007-09 fall. The S&P 500 went from 1,565.15 in October 2007 to 676.53 in March 2009. That's 56.8% gone, more than half the index. The 2000-02 fall took 49.1% and 2020 took 33.9%. In 2022 it went from 4,796.56 to 3,577.03, the mildest of the four. Think about what that means in your account. Hold an index fund through that fall and more than half your money's gone. That's why we don't sit through a fall like this. When the app's market filter turns Red, its worst reading, we're mostly cash. And 56.8% isn't a floor. The next one could go deeper.
questions.lesson_line: More than half the index went in one fall. Don't plan on sitting through the next one.

wrong.The 2000-02 fall: Close, and it was brutal. But 49.1% is less than the 56.8% the index lost in 2007-09.
wrong.The 2020 fall: The fastest, not the deepest. It took 33.9% off the S&P 500 in about a month.
wrong.The 2022 fall: The mildest of the four. The S&P 500 went from 4,796.56 to 3,577.03, nowhere near half.

questions.simple: The 2007-09 fall. The S&P 500 lost 56.8% from its 2007 peak to its 2009 low.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: The 2007-09 bear market grew out of a collapse in ___ prices.
questions.why: Home. Falling home prices helped spark the financial crisis of 2007-08. Markets faced considerable uncertainty about losses on mortgage-related assets. US home prices fell about 30% on average from mid-2006 to mid-2009. The crisis then reached the big firms: Lehman Brothers filed for bankruptcy, and the next day the Fed supported AIG. Oil, tech, gold and food prices were not the trigger here.
questions.lesson_line: 2007-09 started in housing, then spread through the banks to the whole market.
questions.simple: Home, because falling home prices helped set off the 2007-08 financial crisis behind the 2007-09 fall.

questions.q: After the September 11, 2001 attacks, the NYSE didn't reopen for trading until the following Monday.
questions.why: True. The NYSE didn't trade again until Monday, September 17. That's days with no way to sell on the exchange. Your stop orders there couldn't do a thing, because nothing could fill them. Think of it as the biggest gap there is. A stop can't catch an overnight gap, and it can't catch a closed market either. What protects you then is size. A tight stop never makes a monster position safe. Keep each position small enough that you can live with the worst open.
questions.lesson_line: A stop can't sell what can't trade. Size so a closed market can't sink you.
questions.simple: True. The NYSE stayed shut until Monday, September 17, so no stop could fill there until then.

questions.q: Here's the Nasdaq at its March 2000 top. What set off the bear market that came after it?
choices: The US losing its AAA rating
questions.why: The dot-com bubble bursting. By March 2000 the Nasdaq was up 24% on the year, at a record high. Then from the spring it fell hard. Investors got worried about lofty prices in a few hot sectors, and about higher rates. The S&P 500 went on to lose 49.1% by October 2002. When the whole market chases one theme at any price, the unwind can drag everything down for years. That's what this top was. Watch how the leaders act. When they break and can't hold a bounce, I get a lot more careful.
questions.lesson_line: When everyone chases one theme at any price, the unwind can drag the whole market for years.

wrong.A collapse in home prices: That was 2007-09. Falling home prices set off that crisis, not this one.
wrong.A pandemic shutting the economy: That was the 2020 fall, a different story.
wrong.The US losing its AAA rating: That came much later. S&P cut the US rating from AAA to AA+ in a different scare.

questions.simple: The dot-com bubble burst. Tech had run to lofty prices, then fell hard and dragged the market down.

questions.q: When the S&P 500 made this March 2009 low, the recession was already over.
questions.why: False. Stocks bottomed in March 2009. The recession ran until June 2009, going by the NBER, the group that dates US recessions. So price turned about three months before the economy did. The news was still awful the day it bottomed. Wait for the economy to look healthy and the turn is long gone. That's why I watch the index and the leaders, not the headlines. Price tells you first.
questions.lesson_line: Stocks turned while the recession was still on. Price tells you first, the news tells you last.
questions.simple: False. Stocks hit their low in March 2009, and the recession ran until June 2009.

questions.q: For most of 2022 the S&P 500 ground lower. What was behind the selling?
choices: Hot inflation and Fed rate hikes
A collapse in US home prices
The bursting of the dot-com bubble
questions.answer: Hot inflation and Fed rate hikes
questions.why: Hot inflation and Fed rate hikes. Prices were rising at the fastest clip in 40 years, and the Fed kept raising rates to fight it. Russia's invasion of Ukraine piled more doubt on top. No single crash, just a long grind lower with sharp bounces along the way. That kind of market chops up anyone buying every dip. I don't try to trade the Fed. I trade what the market shows me, and in 2022 it showed weakness for months. So smaller size, fewer trades, more cash, until price proves the turn.
questions.lesson_line: A Fed fighting inflation can grind the whole market lower. Trade smaller and let price tell you when it's done.

wrong.A US credit rating downgrade: That was 2011, when S&P cut the US rating from AAA to AA+.
wrong.A collapse in US home prices: That was 2007-09. In 2022 the problem was inflation and rates, not housing.
wrong.The bursting of the dot-com bubble: That was the 2000-2002 bear market. Different era, different cause.

questions.simple: Hot inflation and Fed rate hikes. The Fed raised rates to fight fast-rising prices, and stocks ground lower.

questions.q: You're planning for the next sell-off. Of these S&P 500 falls, which went from high to low the fastest?
questions.why: The 2020 fall. February 19 high to March 23 low, 33 days. The 2007-09 fall took 17 months, and 2000-02 took 30.5 months. 2022 ground on from January into October. A fall that fast gives you no time to think. Stops hit one after another, and gaps jump right past some of them. So the plan has to be in place before it starts. Size you can live with, stops set, cash when the market turns. You won't have time to work it out on the fly.
questions.lesson_line: Some falls take years, one took 33 days. Your plan has to work at both speeds.

wrong.The 2007-09 fall: That one took 17 months, October 2007 to March 2009. Deep, but slow.
wrong.The 2000-02 fall: The slowest of the four, 30.5 months from top to bottom.
wrong.The 2022 fall: That one ground lower from January to October. Months, not 33 days.

questions.simple: The 2020 fall. The S&P 500 went from its high to its low in just 33 days.

questions.q: S&P 500: a 2,930.75 closing high in September 2018, then a 2,351.10 close on Christmas Eve. How far had it fallen?
questions.why: 19.8%. 2,930.75 minus 2,351.10 is 579.65 points. Divide 579.65 by 2,930.75, the high, and you get 19.78%. Round it to 19.8%. Always measure from the high you fell from, close to close. A lot hit stocks that fall: worries about earnings, global growth, trade fights and the Fed. On closes it stopped just short of the 20% most people call a bear market. I don't care much about the label. A near 20% hit to the index feels like a bear in your account, so trade it like one. Smaller, pickier, more cash.
questions.lesson_line: Measure from the closing high. Late 2018 came within a hair of 20%, then turned.
questions.simple: 19.8%. The index fell 579.65 points from 2,930.75, a hair short of 20%.

deeper.trap: The trap is dividing by the low. 579.65 over 2,351.10 gives 24.7% and makes the fall look bigger than it was. A fall is measured from the high you fell from, so the high goes on the bottom: 579.65 over 2,930.75 is 19.78%.

wrong.20.0%: Close, but the closes don't get there. 579.65 over 2,930.75 is 19.78%, a hair under 20%.
wrong.24.7%: That's dividing by the low, 2,351.10. Measure from the high you fell from, 2,930.75.
wrong.80.2%: That's what was left of the index at the low, not how far it fell.

questions.q: Within months of this Christmas Eve 2018 low, the S&P 500 closed back above its old high.
questions.why: True. The S&P 500 closed at 2,351.10 on Christmas Eve 2018. On April 23, 2019 it closed at 2,933.68, back above the 2,930.75 closing high from September. About four months, low to old high. Not every sharp drop turns into a long bear. This one healed fast. So keep working your watchlist while the market falls. Note which names hold up best. When it turns, those are the ones you want to own first.
questions.lesson_line: Not every deep drop becomes a long bear. Keep your list ready for the turn.
questions.simple: True. It closed above its old high on April 23, 2019, about four months after the low.

reasons: first close above the peak is read across one FRED series that rolls off around 2028

questions.q: Summer 2011. The S&P 500 drops hard at the right edge of this chart. What hit it?
choices: A pandemic shutting down the economy
questions.why: The debt-limit fight and Europe's crisis. Stocks fell sharply in late July and early August 2011. Europe's debt crisis, the US debt-ceiling fight and fears of a global slowdown all landed at once. Then S&P cut the US credit rating from AAA to AA+. Scary stuff, but it healed. Stocks roughly won the losses back by early 2012. Headline scares come and go. I size down while it's falling, then look for the names that held up best.
questions.lesson_line: Headline scares come and go. This one healed in months.

wrong.The US housing market's collapse: That was 2007-09. Housing wasn't the story in 2011.
wrong.A pandemic shutting down the economy: That was 2020, when the S&P 500 fell from February 19 to March 23.
wrong.The dot-com tech bubble bursting: That was the 2000-2002 bear market, a decade earlier.

questions.simple: The debt-limit fight and Europe's crisis. Both hit in the summer of 2011, and stocks recovered by early 2012.

reasons: the key rests on one cited fact (f19)

questions.q: Say you bought the Nasdaq at its March 2000 high and held. How long until it closed above that high again?
questions.why: About 15 years. The Nasdaq closed at 5,048.62 on March 10, 2000. Its first close above that came on April 23, 2015, at 5,056.06. In between it bottomed at 1,114.11 on October 9, 2002. Fifteen years to get back to even, and that's a whole index, not one bad stock. Hold and hope isn't a plan. That's why we cut losers small and don't marry a position, however good the story was.
questions.lesson_line: A whole index took about 15 years to get back. Don't hold and hope.

wrong.About 5 months: Way too fast. It didn't even hit bottom until October 9, 2002, at 1,114.11.
wrong.About 2 years: Two years in, it was still falling. The low didn't come until October 9, 2002.
wrong.About 7 years: Seven years on it was still under that high. The first close above it came on April 23, 2015.

questions.simple: About 15 years. The Nasdaq didn't close above its March 2000 high until April 2015.

questions.q: US stocks chop lower from mid-2015 into February 2016 on this chart. What was weighing on them?
choices: A collapse in US home prices
The US losing its AAA rating
questions.why: China worries and falling oil. Doubts about China's currency and its economy set off waves of selling around the world. Oil and other commodities kept falling, and energy and materials stocks dropped hard. A market like this chops you up. Breakouts fail, bounces fade, and small losses pile up. That's when I trade smaller and get pickier. Fewer trades, only the best setups, and more cash.
questions.lesson_line: In a choppy market, trade smaller and pickier. Cash is a position too.

wrong.A collapse in US home prices: That was 2007-09. Housing wasn't the problem here.
wrong.The US losing its AAA rating: That was 2011, when S&P cut the US rating from AAA to AA+.

questions.simple: China worries and falling oil. Trouble abroad hit US stocks, and falling oil hit energy stocks hard.

questions.q: Nasdaq Composite: 5,048.62 at its March 2000 peak, 1,114.11 at its October 2002 low. How far did it fall? Nearest whole %.
questions.why: 78%. From 5,048.62 down to 1,114.11. The tech-heavy index lost more than three quarters of its value.
questions.lesson_line: The bubble's leaders fell hardest. The Nasdaq lost far more than the S&P 500's 49.1%.

questions.q: The S&P 500 peaked on January 3, 2022. This chart runs to its lowest close of the slide. How long did that take?
questions.why: About nine months. The peak close was 4,796.56 on January 3, 2022. The lowest close was 3,577.03 on October 12. That's nine months of grinding lower, with sharp bounces along the way. Five weeks was the 2020 pace. 17 months was 2007-09, and 30 months was 2000-02. A slow grind like this wears you down more than a crash does. You keep thinking the bottom's in. Let the market prove it's turned before you press.
questions.lesson_line: This bear ground lower for about nine months. Let the market prove it's turned before you press.

wrong.About 5 weeks: That was the 2020 pace, 33 days from February 19 to March 23.

questions.simple: About nine months. The index peaked on January 3, 2022 and made its lowest close on October 12.

reasons: length computed from two FRED closes

questions.story: August 24, 2015. S&P futures hit their 5% limit down before the open. You own an S&P 500 fund with a sell stop 6% under Friday's close. It opens 5.2% below that close and is down 7.8% by 9:35.
questions.q: What happens to your stop order?
choices: It becomes a market order and sells
It fills at exactly your stop price
It waits for the price to recover
It cancels when trading gets too wild
questions.answer: It becomes a market order and sells
questions.why: It turns into a market order and sells. Your 6% stop is a trigger, not a promised price. SPY opened 5.2% down, then traded through your 6% line within minutes, so the order went to market. In a fast open it takes whatever's there, and that could be near the 7.8% low. By 9:40 SPY was back above its open, and it closed down only 4.2%. So the stop could have sold you within a hair of the worst print of the day. That's why, when a big gap down opens near my stop, I handle it by hand. The low of the first half hour becomes my new stop. If that low takes the loss past twice what I planned to risk, I'm out.
questions.lesson_line: A stop is a trigger, not a price. In a wild open it can sell you near the low.

wrong.It fills at exactly your stop price: That's the mistake most people make. Once the stop triggers, you get the next price, and here that could be well under 6%.
wrong.It waits for the price to recover: A stop doesn't wait. One quick flush through your price sets it off, even if SPY bounces right after. It did.
wrong.It cancels when trading gets too wild: Nothing cancels it. A wild open is exactly when a stop fills far from its price.

questions.simple: It turns into a market order and sells at the next price, which can be well below your stop.

deeper.trap: The trap is thinking your stop sells at 6% down. It only starts the sale. The market order then takes the next prices, and this fund was down as much as 7.8% by 9:35. By 9:40 it was back above its open, and it closed down 4.2%. FINRA warns that a short, sharp move can trigger a stop, and the price may rebound afterwards.

reasons: owner flag raised: the gap rule B20 sits close to this case (not scored)

questions.story: 2022. The S&P 500 has fallen for months. Then it rallies for two straight months, from 3,666.77 in June to 4,305.20. It feels like the bottom's in.
questions.q: Where did the index go from here?
choices: Gave it all back and made a new low
Went on to make a new record that year
Held its gains and went sideways
Dipped back but held above its low
questions.answer: Gave it all back and made a new low
questions.why: It gave it all back and made a new low. From 4,305.20 on August 16, the S&P 500 slid to 3,577.03 by October 12. That's under June's 3,666.77. The January record of 4,796.56 wasn't topped until January 19, 2024. And look where the rally stalled: right up at a falling long-term moving average. Rallies inside a bear are fast and convincing, and that's how they pull people back in. A big bounce isn't a bottom. You only know the bottom in hindsight. So take the setups that work, keep your stops tight, and don't go all in on a bounce.
questions.lesson_line: A big bounce inside a bear isn't a bottom. You only know the bottom in hindsight.

wrong.Went on to make a new record that year: No. The January 2022 record of 4,796.56 wasn't topped until January 2024.
wrong.Held its gains and went sideways: It gave the whole rally back and more, closing at 3,577.03 on October 12.
wrong.Dipped back but held above its low: It didn't hold. 3,577.03 on October 12 is under the June 16 close of 3,666.77.

questions.simple: It made a new low. The rally faded and the index closed under its June low by October.

deeper.trap: The trap is reading a two-month rally off the low as proof the bottom is in. In 2022 it was not. The rally from 3,666.77 to 4,305.20 gave way to a close of 3,577.03 on October 12. S&P Dow Jones Indices marks a bear market's end at the low only once the index later rises 20%. So the bottom is known only in hindsight.

reasons: key read across one FRED series that rolls off around 2032

questions.q: From 1,565.15 in 2007, the S&P 500 fell to 676.53 in 2009. What gain gets it back to the old high?
questions.why: 131%. 1,565.15 minus 676.53 is 888.62 points. Divide that by 676.53, where the climb starts, and you get 131%. A 56.8% loss means the index has to more than double just to get back to even. The gain you need grows much faster than the loss. That's the math behind why we cut losers small. Those who control their drawdown best are best. Simple as that.
questions.lesson_line: Big losses need far bigger gains to fix. Cut them small.
questions.simple: 131%. After a 56.8% loss, what's left has to more than double to get back to the old high.

deeper.trap: The trap is thinking a 56.8% loss needs only a 56.8% gain to repair. Gains start from the smaller base that is left. So the climb back from 676.53 to 1,565.15 is 131%, more than twice the loss.

wrong.57%: That's the loss, not the fix. The gain starts from the smaller number that's left, 676.53, so it has to be much bigger.
wrong.43%: That's about how much of the index was left at the low, not the gain you need.
wrong.231%: That counts the 676.53 you start with as part of the gain. The gain on top of it is 131%.

questions.q: The official end date of a US recession comes out the same month the recession ends.
questions.why: False, not even close. The NBER, the group that dates US recessions, names the end long after the fact. The November 2001 end was announced on July 17, 2003. The June 2009 end came out September 20, 2010. The April 2020 end came out July 19, 2021. More than a year late every time. The S&P 500 had bottomed back on March 23, 2020. By the time it's official, price moved long ago. Trade what the market is showing you now.
questions.lesson_line: By the time a recession's end is official, price moved long ago. Trade what's in front of you.
questions.simple: False. The official end date comes out more than a year late, like in 2001, 2009 and 2020.

deeper.trap: The trap is waiting for the official all-clear. The S&P 500's 2020 fall ended on March 23, 2020. The NBER named April 2020 as the recession's end only on July 19, 2021. By then price had moved for more than a year.

questions.story: A buddy says every big market fall looks like 2008: more than a year of sliding, and stocks cut in half.
questions.q: What does the record since 2000 say about that?
choices: Falls vary a lot in speed and depth
Most big falls are over within weeks
Every big fall stops near a 20% drop
The slow slides turn out the mildest
questions.answer: Falls vary a lot in speed and depth
questions.why: Falls come in every speed and depth. 2020 took 33 days and cut the S&P 500 by 33.9%. The 2000-02 fall took 30.5 months and cut it 49.1%. The 2007-09 fall took 17 months and cut it 56.8%. So 2008 is one shape, not the template. Plan only for the last crash you remember and the next one catches you off guard. Tell your buddy the honest answer: nobody knows which kind is next. What you control is your stops, your size and how fast you go to cash.
questions.lesson_line: Don't plan for one kind of fall. Plan for fast and slow, shallow and deep.

wrong.The slow slides turn out the mildest: The reverse here. 2000-02 took 30.5 months and fell 49.1%, more than 2020's 33.9% in 33 days.
wrong.Every big fall stops near a 20% drop: No. 2020 fell 33.9%, and 2007-09 went all the way to 56.8%.
wrong.Most big falls are over within weeks: Only 2020 was. 2000-02 took 30.5 months and 2007-09 took 17.

questions.simple: Falls vary a lot. 2020 dropped 33.9% in 33 days, while 2000-02 took 30.5 months to drop 49.1%.

deeper.trap: The trap is planning only for the last crash you remember. The 2007-09 fall took 17 months. The 2020 fall took 33 days. The 2000-02 fall ground on for 30.5 months. One plan has to handle every speed.

questions.story: Fall 2002. The economy has been growing for most of a year. But accounting scandals and profit warnings keep hitting stocks, and the index just made a new low.
questions.q: What's this low telling you about stocks and the economy?
choices: Stocks can slide as the economy grows
Stocks bottom before the economy does
A growing economy stops a stock slide
A new low means a recession is here
questions.answer: Stocks can slide as the economy grows
questions.why: Stocks can slide while the economy grows. The 2001 recession ended in November 2001, and the economy kept growing through 2002. Stocks fell anyway. Accounting scandals, profit warnings and tension abroad drove the slide. By early October, indexes sat at their lowest since spring 1997. They turned in late October, when third-quarter earnings came in better than feared. In 2009 stocks bottomed before the recession ended. Here they bottomed almost a year after it ended. Two different clocks. So don't use the economy to time the market. Read the chart in front of you.
questions.lesson_line: The economy and the market keep different clocks. Trade the chart, not the GDP headlines.

wrong.Stocks bottom before the economy does: Sometimes, like in 2009. Here the low came almost a year after the recession ended.
wrong.A growing economy stops a stock slide: It didn't here. The economy grew through 2002 while scandals and profit warnings drove stocks lower.
wrong.A new low means a recession is here: Not this time. The economy kept growing through 2002.

questions.simple: Stocks can slide while the economy grows. In 2002 they made new lows during a recovery.

deeper.trap: The trap is reading the economy to call the market. In 2002 the economy was growing, yet scandals and profit warnings kept pushing stocks lower until early October. The turn came in late October, when third-quarter earnings came in better than feared.
